8.title: not "suffering"
8.hook: not "suffering" — the wobble in the wheel; the itch under everything
8.howItsDone: Buddhists learn dukkha as the first of the four noble truths, and many teachers invite students simply to recognize it in daily life, the aches, the endings, the restlessness, without adding blame or panic.

segments.voice: Yesterday: rebirth, one flame lighting the next. Your line was one flame lights the next. Week two opens the four truths one at a time, starting with the first one's word. Day eight.

You finally get the thing. The new phone, the weekend off, the apartment with the good light. And for a day or two it's wonderful. Then, very quietly, something starts to itch. The phone has a scratch. The weekend is already half over on Saturday night. The light is great, but the neighbors are loud. Nothing is wrong, exactly. It just doesn't quite sit right. There's a word for that. It's usually translated as suffering, which is why so many people think Buddhism is gloomy. But the word is smaller and stranger than suffering. It's about a wheel.
screen: `YOU FINALLY GET THE THING.` → `THEN, QUIETLY, AN ITCH.` → `A WORD ABOUT A WHEEL.`

segments.voice: Dukkha. It's the first big word of the Buddha's teaching, and it's almost impossible to translate. Suffering is the usual choice. Some translators say stress, or unsatisfactoriness, which is accurate and nobody can say it twice. So teachers often reach for a picture instead. A popular explanation splits the word in two. Du, bad. Kha, a hole, and in particular the hole in the middle of a wheel, where the axle goes. A cart with a badly fitted wheel still rolls. You still get where you're going. But every turn has a little jolt in it. That's dukkha. Its opposite is sukha, a good axle hole, which came to mean happiness: a smooth ride. Scholars aren't sure that's where the word really comes from. But the picture has stuck because it fits. Buddhist teachers describe three layers of it. The first is plain pain: a toothache, a breakup, a funeral. Nobody needs that explained. The second is the pain of change: the good thing that's already ending while you're enjoying it, the Sunday evening feeling. The third is the subtlest: the low hum of everything being conditioned, dependent, never quite solid enough to rest on. The itch under everything. Seeing the wobble clearly is not the same as being crushed by it. Often it's a relief. Oh. It's not just me. It's the wheel.
screen: `DUKKHA — HARD TO TRANSLATE.` · `DU, BAD. KHA, THE AXLE HOLE.` · `PAIN, CHANGE, THE HUM UNDERNEATH.` · `IT'S NOT JUST ME.` · then, large: `THE WOBBLE IN THE WHEEL.`

segments.voice: Today the bell gives you a little longer: about forty-five seconds. Notice one small wobble right now. A tight shoulder. A worry about later. A message you haven't answered. Don't fix it. Just name it: this too. Then notice that the wobble and the breath are both here, and the breath is still coming in and going out. Stay with both until the bell.
Dukkha. Not only suffering: the wobble in the wheel, the itch under things, the ride that's never perfectly smooth. Eighth word.
Your line: this too. Two small words for the small wobbles, and the big ones. Day eight.

fork.reveal: the pain of change: the good thing that's already ending while you're still in it. teachers name it as the second layer.

original.note: Pali: the unsatisfactoriness of things. Sanskrit duḥkha; its opposite is sukha.

trapdoor: what you thought: Buddhism says life is suffering.
what it means: there's a wobble in the wheel. pain, change, and a quiet itch under everything. naming it is the start of healing it.

what a scholar hears: dukkha, often explained as du + kha, a badly fitted axle hole. the etymology is popular but debated; the threefold division (pain, change, conditioned things) comes from the discourses and commentaries.

9.title: craving
9.hook: craving — wanting things to be other than they are
9.howItsDone: Buddhists learn the second noble truth as the arising of dukkha from craving, and in meditation practice noticing wanting and aversion as they come up, without acting on them right away.

segments.voice: Yesterday: dukkha, the wobble in the wheel. Your line was this too. Today, the second truth: where the wobble comes from. Day nine.

You're in a slow line at the grocery store. The person ahead is paying in coins. Counting them. Out loud. For a lot of people, something happens in the body. The jaw tightens. The weight shifts. A little voice starts narrating: why is this line always the slow one. Now here's the odd thing. The line is just a line. It isn't hurting anyone. What hurts, looked at closely, is the gap between the line that is and the line that's wanted. That gap has a name. The Buddha said it's where the wobble comes from.
screen: `THE SLOW LINE.` → `THE JAW TIGHTENS.` → `THE GAP BETWEEN IS AND WANT.`

segments.voice: The second noble truth is about where dukkha comes from. In Pali it's samudaya, arising, origin. And the Buddha's answer is one word: tanha. It literally means thirst. Not a polite preference. Thirst. The dry-mouthed, leaning-forward kind that makes you reach before you think. In the first sermon he names three thirsts. The thirst for pleasant things: the next bite, the next scroll, the next thing to buy. The thirst to be something: to be seen, to be right, to last. And the thirst not to be: to make something go away, to disappear from a feeling, to wish this moment weren't happening. Some teachers read that third thirst widely: wanting something gone is a thirst too. On that reading, the grocery line is thirst of the third kind. Here's a careful point. Buddhism doesn't say every wish is a problem. Teachers use a different Pali word, chanda, for a wish or will that can be wholesome: the wish to be kind, the intention to practice, the will to get up and help someone. What the second truth names is the grasping kind. The kind that insists: this should be different, right now, or I can't be okay. So letting go of craving doesn't mean loving people less. The Buddha taught families how to care for each other. The trouble is the grip, not the care. And here's why it's hopeful, not harsh. If the wobble came from the world, you'd be stuck. You can't make every line fast. But if it comes from the thirst, there's something you can actually work with. The thirst is closer to home.
screen: `SAMUDAYA — WHERE IT COMES FROM.` · `TANHA — LITERALLY, THIRST.` · `WANTING MORE, TO BE, NOT TO BE.` · `NOT EVERY WISH IS CRAVING.` · then, large: `THE WANTING IS THE WOBBLE.`

segments.voice: The bell gives you about forty-five seconds. Find something you want right now. Food, a message, for this lesson to end. Anything. Feel where the wanting lives in your body: the chest, the hands, the jaw. Don't get rid of it, and don't follow it. Just notice that it's a feeling, and that it's thirsty, and keep breathing beside it.
Tanha. Thirst: the second truth's answer to where dukkha comes from, wanting things to be other than they are. Ninth word.
Your line: the wanting is the wobble. The line was only ever a line. Day nine, done.

trapdoor: what you thought: Buddhists aren't supposed to want anything.

what a scholar hears: tanha in three forms, for sense pleasure (kama), for being (bhava) and for non-being (vibhava), named in the Dhammacakkappavattana Sutta; chanda, wish or intention, can be wholesome.

Sigalovada Sutta (Digha Nikaya 31): care between parents, children, partners and friends

10.title: it can stop
10.hook: it can stop; not a heaven you go to, a fire with nothing left to burn
10.howItsDone: Buddhists speak of nirvana as the end of craving and of dukkha; in Theravada it is the goal of the path, and Mahayana traditions describe awakening in their own terms, while everyday practice keeps attention on letting go.

segments.voice: Yesterday: tanha, thirst, the second truth. Your line was the wanting is the wobble. A diagnosis, then a cause. Today, the third truth. Day ten.

A headache that's sat behind the eyes all afternoon finally lifts. Nobody marked the minute it arrived. Sometimes the leaving is the only part anyone notices. If the Buddha's teaching stopped at the first two truths, a diagnosis and a cause, it would be a heavy teaching. It doesn't stop there. The third truth says the wobble can end, and the word for that ending is one you've likely heard: as the name of a band, a kind of heaven, a perfect afternoon. It's none of those.
screen: `THE HEADACHE LIFTS.` → `A DIAGNOSIS. A CAUSE.` → `AND THEN: IT CAN END.`

segments.voice: The third noble truth is nirodha. Cessation. Stopping. In the first sermon it's put simply: when the thirst fades away completely, when it's let go and released, dukkha ends. Remove the cause, and what it causes stops. The name for that ending is nirvana, in Sanskrit, or nibbana, in Pali. Teachers link the word to a flame going out, the way a lamp goes out when there's no more fuel. That's the image. Not a place you go. The fire of craving, with nothing left to burn. People sometimes hear that and think it sounds like nothingness. The texts don't describe it that way. The Dhammapada lists the best things there are: "Health is the greatest of gifts, contentment the best riches; trust is the best of relationships, Nirvana the highest happiness." Happiness. Not blankness. And there's an exchange in the discourses that uses the same fire. A wanderer asks the Buddha where a fully awakened person goes after death. The Buddha asks him: when a fire goes out in front of you, which direction did it go? North? South? The man admits the question doesn't fit. The fire just went out. The Buddha says this question is like that one. Buddhist traditions describe nirvana in different words, and the texts often say what it isn't. But the third truth itself is simple. The wobble is real. And it isn't permanent.
screen: `NIRODHA — STOPPING.` · `NIRVANA — A FLAME GOING OUT.` · `THE HIGHEST HAPPINESS.` · `WHICH WAY DID THE FIRE GO?` · then, large: `THERE IS AN END.`

segments.voice: The bell gives you about forty-five seconds. Notice any small wanting that's here. Then any small ache. Then look for a moment, even a flicker, where neither is pulling at you. A gap. A small quiet between two thoughts. It might be tiny. When it closes, wait for the next one. That tiny thing is what the third truth is pointing at.
Nirvana. The third truth's word: when the thirst ends, dukkha ends. The flame with nothing left to burn. Tenth word.
Your line: there is an end. Not a place to get to; a fire that's gone out. See you tomorrow.

fork.reveal: he asks about the fire. north, south, east, west? the question doesn't fit, and the Buddha says the wanderer's question is like that one.

original.note: Pali: nibbāna, the going out of a flame. Sanskrit: nirvāṇa. The third noble truth is nirodha, cessation.

trapdoor: what you thought: nirvana is Buddhist heaven.
what it means: the ending of craving, and with it dukkha: the flame with nothing left to burn.

what a scholar hears: nirodha, cessation; nibbana, from a root meaning to blow or go out. in the Aggivacchagotta Sutta (MN 72) the Buddha refuses the question of where an awakened one goes, using the extinguished fire.

11.title: a path
11.hook: a path — eight parts, a life
11.tomorrow: five, and they read like kindness
11.howItsDone: Buddhists practice the eightfold path as a whole way of life: keeping ethical precepts in speech, action and work, meditating, and studying the teaching; the eight-spoked wheel, the dharmachakra, is one of Buddhism's most common symbols.

segments.voice: Yesterday: nirvana, the flame going out. Your line was there is an end. Today, the fourth truth: how to get there. Day eleven.

A mechanic tells you the car has a problem, and walks off. A friend says you seem stressed, and changes the subject. Being told what's wrong and then left there is almost worse than not knowing. The first three truths could have been like that. There is dukkha. It comes from thirst. It can end. Great. How? The Buddha didn't leave it there. The fourth truth isn't an idea at all. It's directions. And they aren't a one-time fix, like a pill. They're something you walk, every day, for a life.
screen: `THE PROBLEM, THEN SILENCE.` → `GREAT. HOW?` → `THE FOURTH TRUTH IS DIRECTIONS.`

segments.voice: The fourth noble truth is magga, the path. The way that leads to the end of dukkha. It has eight parts, so it's called the noble eightfold path. Here they are, quickly. Right view. Right intention. Right speech. Right action. Right livelihood. Right effort. Right mindfulness, the sati from day three. Right concentration. The word translated right is samma, and it's gentler than it sounds in English. It means whole, complete, well-tuned, the way a chord is right. Not right as opposed to wrong answers on a test. Right the way a thing fits. In one of the old discourses, a nun named Dhammadinna sorts the eight into three bundles. Wisdom: seeing clearly and meaning well. Conduct: how you speak, act and earn a living. And meditation: effort, mindfulness, concentration. Notice what that means. Most of the path isn't sitting on a cushion. It's how you talk to your sister and how you make your money. And here's what people often get wrong. The eight aren't steps you finish one at a time, like levels. They're more like the eight spokes of a wheel, and many Buddhists read the eight-spoked wheel that way. They turn together. A little honesty helps meditation. A little meditation helps honesty. One old verse says it plainly: "The best of ways is the eightfold; the best of truths the four words." The four words are the four truths you now know. The eightfold way is how you walk them.
screen: `MAGGA — THE PATH.` · `EIGHT PARTS, EACH ONE SAMMA.` · `WISDOM, CONDUCT, MEDITATION.` · `SPOKES OF A WHEEL, NOT STEPS.` · then, large: `THE BEST OF WAYS IS THE EIGHTFOLD.`

segments.voice: The bell gives you about forty-five seconds. Sit comfortably. Pick just one spoke of the wheel. Maybe speech: one thing you'd like to say more kindly. Maybe action: one small harm you'd like to skip. Maybe livelihood: one moment at work you'd like to do honestly. Hold that one spoke in mind, and breathe with it. Nobody walks all eight at once. One step is still walking.
The eightfold path. The fourth noble truth: eight parts, wisdom, conduct and meditation, turning together like a wheel. Eleventh word.
Your line: walk. The truths are something you walk, not something you believe. Day eleven.

screen: `DAY 11 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: FIVE, AND THEY READ LIKE KINDNESS.`

12.title: five, and they read like kindness
12.hook: five, and they read like kindness
12.howItsDone: Lay Buddhists often recite the five precepts in Pali after taking refuge in the Buddha, the Dhamma and the Sangha, at temple services, festivals and at home; some keep eight precepts on observance days.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the eightfold path, eight spokes turning together. Your line was walk. Today, the conduct spokes, in five short lines. Day twelve.

When people hear a religion has rules, they brace. They picture a long list of thou-shalt-nots, somebody stern at the top, and a lot of guilt. Buddhism has a short list too. Five lines. Buddhists say them at temples and at home, often every week, some every day, in a temple in Sri Lanka or a living room in Los Angeles. But read them closely and they don't sound like a list of rules. They sound like a promise to be easy to live next to.
screen: `A RELIGION HAS RULES.` → `FIVE LINES, SAID EVERY WEEK.` → `EASY TO LIVE NEXT TO.`

segments.voice: The precepts. In Pali, sila: conduct, virtue, the way you live. There are five for lay Buddhists. Not to kill or harm living beings. Not to take what isn't given. Not to cause harm through sex. Not to speak falsely. And not to take intoxicants that cloud the mind. That's the list. Now listen to how they're actually said. Each one is phrased the same way: I undertake the training rule to refrain from harming living beings. I undertake the training rule to refrain from taking what is not given. And so on. Notice the words. I undertake. Nobody is ordering anyone. You take them on yourself. And training rule. Not a law, not a commandment. Something you practice, fail at sometimes, and pick up again, the way you'd train for a race. There's a teaching in the discourses that turns the whole thing around. It calls the five precepts five great gifts. When you keep them, the Buddha says, you give freedom from fear to countless beings. Everyone near you can relax. They don't have to worry you'll hurt them, rob them, betray them, lie to them, or lose control. And because you give them safety, you get to share in that safety too. That's why they read like kindness. They aren't about keeping yourself pure. They're about everyone else being able to breathe around you. Buddhists hold them in different ways. Some take all five for life. Some take them fresh on holy days. Monks and nuns take many more.
screen: `SILA — HOW YOU LIVE.` · `FIVE LINES FOR LAY BUDDHISTS.` · `I UNDERTAKE THE TRAINING RULE.` · `FIVE GREAT GIFTS: NO FEAR.` · then, large: `EASY TO LIVE NEXT TO.`

segments.voice: The bell gives you about forty-five seconds. Think about the five: not harming, not taking, not betraying, not lying, not clouding the mind. Don't grade yourself. Just ask which one would make the biggest difference to the people around you this week. Picture someone near you feeling a little safer because of it, and rest there.
The precepts. Five training rules, taken on freely, that give everyone around you freedom from fear. Twelfth word.
Your line: do less harm. It's a training rule, not a test you pass or fail. That's day twelve.

13.title: impermanence
13.hook: impermanence; the leaf, the mood, the year
13.howItsDone: Buddhists reflect on anicca in meditation by watching breath, sensations and thoughts arise and pass, and in daily life by recalling that all conditioned things change; some traditions use images like falling leaves, candles and sand mandalas swept away after completion.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the precepts, five training rules that give others freedom from fear. Your line was do less harm. Today, the first of three marks. Day thirteen.

A leaf in October. Last spring it was a tight green bud. In summer it was so ordinary nobody noticed it. Now it's red and gold and loose on the branch, and next week it'll be on the sidewalk. Set this morning's mood beside this one. Look at last year: a worry that kept someone up in March can be hard to even recall by fall. The leaf, the mood, the year. They're all doing the same thing, at different speeds. They're passing. The Buddha asked people to look at that, closely, until they saw it.

Anicca. In Pali, nicca means permanent, lasting, constant. Put an a in front and you get the opposite: not lasting. Impermanence. It's the first of what Buddhists call the three marks of existence, the three things true of everything that's made of parts and conditions. Anicca, impermanence. Dukkha, which you already know. And anatta, which is tomorrow. The Dhammapada puts the first one in four words: "All created things perish." Now, that sounds obvious. Everyone knows things change. But here's the catch. It's easy to know it the way we know the sun is a star: true, and no help at all on a Tuesday. A good mood gets held as if it'll stay. A bad week feels like forever. An ending still startles. So the Buddha didn't teach anicca as a fact to agree with. He taught it as something to see, again and again, in small things, until it sinks in. Watch a breath: it comes, and goes. Watch a thought: it arrives, and leaves. Watch a sound fade away. And there's another side to it. Impermanence isn't only sad news. It's what makes change possible at all. If things were permanent, grief would never soften. A bad habit would never break. The seed would never grow. The same fact that takes the leaf in October brings the bud in April.
screen: `ANICCA — NOT LASTING.` · `THE FIRST OF THREE MARKS.` · `ALL CREATED THINGS PERISH.` · `WHY GRIEF CAN SOFTEN.` · then, large: `THIS PASSES.`

segments.voice: The bell gives you about forty-five seconds. Watch something pass. Start with the breath: notice that each one begins, and ends, and is never quite the same as the last. Then notice sounds around you, arriving and leaving. If a feeling comes up, watch that too. You're not trying to hold anything or push anything away. Just watching things come and go, like leaves.
Anicca. Impermanence, the first of the three marks. Everything made of parts is passing, the hard things and the good ones. Thirteenth word.
Your line: this passes. The leaf in October, and the bud in April. That's thirteen.

trapdoor: what you thought: everything changes. obviously.
what it means: a fact easy to agree with and hard to live by, practiced until it's seen in every breath, mood and year.
what a scholar hears: anicca, the first of the tilakkhaṇa, the three marks. Dhammapada 277 pairs it with dukkha and anatta in verses 278 and 279.

14.title: not-self
14.hook: not-self — who's actually in there? (the question, not the answer)
14.tomorrow: a word for wishing well on people you don't like
14.howItsDone: Buddhists explore anatta through meditation, observing body, feelings and thoughts without identifying with them, and through study; Theravada teaching centers on the five aggregates, while Mahayana schools also teach it through emptiness.

segments.voice: Yesterday: anicca, impermanence, the first mark. Your line was this passes. Today, the third mark, and the question under day seven's flame. Day fourteen.

Try this. Say the word I, and then try to point to it. A finger usually goes to the chest. But is that it? The body at six is not the body now. Opinions change. Taste in music changes. A mood can turn twice before lunch. So who's the I that stayed the same through all of that? It's an old question. The Buddha asked it too, and his answer is well known and often misunderstood. Today we're taking the question, not the answer.
screen: `SAY "I", THEN POINT TO IT.` → `BODY, OPINIONS, MOODS, ALL CHANGING.` → `WHO'S ACTUALLY IN THERE?`

segments.voice: Anatta. Atta means self, the unchanging core, the owner. An-atta: not-self. It's the third mark of existence, after anicca and dukkha. Here's how the Buddha is remembered teaching it, to the same five companions from the deer park; tradition counts it as his second discourse. He goes through what a person is made of. The texts count five heaps: the body, feelings, perceptions, mental formations, and consciousness. And he asks about each one. Is the body permanent or impermanent? Impermanent. Is what's impermanent something you can rest on, or does it wobble? It wobbles. Then is it right to say of it: this is mine, this is what I am, this is my self? No. And he goes through all five the same way. It's not a lecture. It's a series of questions. Look, and see. Another discourse keeps the question open in a different way. A wanderer asks the Buddha straight out: is there a self? The Buddha is silent. Is there no self? Silent again. Later he explains to his attendant Ananda that either answer would have led the man into a wrong view. Some teachers say anatta is less a doctrine to hold than a way of looking: don't cling to anything as me or mine, and see what happens. Buddhist schools talk about this in different ways. Theravada teachers stress the five heaps and the practice of seeing them as not-self. Mahayana teachers speak of emptiness, and some schools of a buddha-nature in every being. Who's in there? Keep the question open.
